submission.natural_language_explanation: N225+ fires at phrase boundaries in running prose: activation is strongest on the token that closes a phrase - the token whose successor is a comma, full stop, semicolon, closing bracket or a linking preposition/conjunction ('of', 'to', 'in', 'and', 'but', 'than') - and grows with the length of the unit since the previous punctuation (13% of such tokens exceed half-max after 5+ tokens vs 5% right after punctuation), while falling to the floor when the same word sits mid-phrase (before a word continuation or a determiner+noun), just after punctuation, or after a matched word-order edit ('the weather was dry' 2.11 -> 'the dry weather was' 0.21). Its write only nudges high-frequency function words (' the' +1.3 nats, then ' it', ' your', ' these') and suppresses rare word-continuation fragments, leaving the top-1 token unchanged at 89% of peaks (protocol lookahead KL 9e-4, so retrospective); mid-word fragments of byte-mangled non-Latin text also peak and remain an unexplained leftover.

top_examples.text:
Recently Viewed Items

Your Shopping Cart

q98 - Q98 Pipe

Scan this QR Code using your mobile device to be directed to the product page.

The Q98 is the pipe of choice for most stock reed engine applications. The Q98 power band has tremendous mid range and top end. The normal tunable head pipe length is 9 to 9 3/4". Top RPM will vary depending on the application but generally on a speedway track, gear for 15,700 to 16,400. On sprint applications 18,000 with a short head pipe is not out of its RPM capabilities. Clutch engagement is 10,800 to 11,000 at short head pipe lengths and 11,000 to 11,200 at longer head pipe lengths.

Crash Nitro Kart

Crash Nitro Kart, released in Japan as Crash Bandicoot: Bakusou! Nitro Kart (クラッシュバンディクー ： 爆走 ！ ニトロカート Kurasshu Bandikū: Bakusō! Nitoro Kāto lit. "Crash Bandicoot: Let's Go! Nitro Kart!"), is a 2003 racing video game developed by Vicarious Visions and Universal Interactive. It is published by Vivendi Universal Games (along with Konami in the Japanese release) for the PlayStation 2, Nintendo GameCube, Xbox, Game Boy Advance and N-Gage. The home console and Game Boy Advance versions were released in North America on November 11, 2003, in Europe on November 28, 2003, in Australia on December 4, 2003; and in Japan on July 8, 2004 for the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo Gamecube and August 26, 2004 for the Game Boy Advance version. The PlayStation 2 version was rereleased for the Sony Greatest Hits line-up on December 2004 and for the Platinum Range on August 27, 2004. The Xbox version was rereleased for the Platinum Family Hits line-up in 2005. The N-Gage version of the game was released in Europe on June 30, 2004 and in North America on July 28, 2004. The mobile phone version was released on September 20, 2004. The PlayStation 2 version was re-released in the three-disc "Crash Bandicoot Action Pack" compilation (alongside Crash Twinsanity and Crash Tag Team Racing) in the United States on June 12, 2007 and in Europe on July 20, 2007.

The game is the ninth installment in the Crash Bandicoot series. It is an indirect sequel to Crash Team Racing and the first game in the series to have full motion video. The game's story centers on the abduction of Crash Bandicoot, along with other characters in the series, by the ruthless dictator Emperor Velo XXVII. Threatening to destroy the Earth if they refuse, he forces them all to race in his gigantic coliseum for the entertainment of his subjects. Crash Nitro Kart received mixed reviews, with reviews varying from version to version. The home console version was met with generally fair reviews. Reviewers dismissed the game as a generic kart racer, but commented positively on its "power slide" system. The Game Boy Advance version earned slightly better reviews than the console version, while reviews for the N-Gage version were middling, with much of the criticism going to the game's "tunnel vision".

Gameplay

Crash Nitro Kart is a racing game in which the player controls characters from the Crash Bandicoot universe, most of whom race in karts. While racing, the player can accelerate, steer, reverse, brake, hop or use weapons and power-ups with the game controller's analog stick and buttons. Four distinct types of crates are scattered throughout the tracks and arenas of Crash Nitro Kart. "Item Crates" are marked with a question mark (?) and usually come in sets of four. The player can obtain a weapon or power-up by driving through an Item Crate and breaking it apart. The player can only carry one weapon or power-up at a time. adversarial_test_results.prompt: Last week was cold. A dry wind blew. Snow fell, they said, by noon. Roads closed fast.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' dry' as an attributive adjective mid-phrase before its noun, with every punctuation-to-punctuation unit at four tokens or fewer; the hypothesis predicts the floor for mid-phrase positions and short units.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Each small step helps. The result, they said, was satisfactory. Nothing broke. We left early.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' small' before its noun and ' satisfactory' at a full stop but after only a two-token unit, so the hypothesis's mid-phrase and length claims both predict no peak.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The level ground, we saw, lay ahead. We walked. The crew came late. Nobody spoke.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' level' as an adjective directly before a noun rather than at a phrase boundary; the hypothesis predicts the floor for a mid-phrase word.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Her feet hurt, she said, all day. The boots, she thought, were too tight. She sat down.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' feet' as a body-part noun followed by its verb, mid-phrase; the hypothesis predicts the floor away from phrase-final position.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They received gifts, she said, all week. The cards, they thought, looked nice. Nobody wrote back.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' received' as a verb taking an object so it is not phrase-final; the hypothesis predicts the floor for this mid-phrase use.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He goes home, they say, by bus. The route, she thinks, is short. It works well.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' goes' before the adverbial ' home', inside a phrase rather than clause-final; the hypothesis predicts the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The box came, from the coast, by train. The trip, we thought, was long. We slept.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' from' immediately after punctuation and followed by the determiner ' the', inside a prepositional phrase; the hypothesis predicts the floor for a word just after punctuation and mid-phrase.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She sat, by the window, for hours. The rain, she said, had stopped. We left.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' by' immediately after punctuation and before a determiner in an interpolated phrase with short units; the hypothesis predicts the floor for a mid-phrase preposition.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The rainy season, they say, starts soon. The fields, we hope, will fill. Farmers wait.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' rainy' attributively before ' season' on the weather topic of the examples; the hypothesis predicts the floor for a mid-phrase adjective.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A satisfactory answer, she said, came late. The judge, we heard, agreed. Nobody cheered.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' satisfactory' before a noun, mid-phrase; the hypothesis predicts the floor despite the word being one of the claimed activating tokens.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The dry weather, they said, was poor. The crops, we saw, failed. Prices rose.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the matched word-order edit in the direction the hypothesis reports as the low case: ' dry' sits before its noun in 'the dry weather' instead of closing the clause.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The rainy forecast, we heard, was wrong. The picnic, they said, went on. Kids played.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Same word-order edit for ' rainy': the trigger precedes a noun rather than a comma, which the hypothesis says drops activation toward the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The river level rose, they said, all night. Sandbags held. Two feet, he said, of snow fell.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' level' as a mid-phrase noun before its verb and ' feet' at a comma after only a two-token unit on the flood topic; the growth-with-unit-length claim predicts no peak.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Apples, pears, plums, figs, dates, grapes filled the crate. The fruit, she said, looked fresh. We bought some.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Delimiter control: a comma-separated list where every comma follows a one- or two-token item, so the hypothesis's length rule predicts no phrase-closing peak despite heavy punctuation.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: # read file, skip header, parse rows, then stop. # the loop, he said, ends soon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests a comment-like fragment outside running prose where every unit is two or three tokens long; the hypothesis predicts the floor for non-prose short units.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: O rio, disseram, subiu. O nível, disseram, era alto.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Portuguese near-miss on the river/flood topic: every punctuation boundary follows a two- to three-token unit (after sub-word splitting), so the hypothesis's growth-with-unit-length claim predicts no peak in this same-script other language.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: La banda, dijeron, tocó. El sonido, oímos, fue claro. Nadie se fue.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Spanish near-miss on the music topic: every punctuation boundary follows a two- to four-token unit (after sub-word splitting), so the hypothesis's short-unit floor predicts no peak in another language written in the same script.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Bring paper; bring pens; bring tape; bring string; bring bread. The list, she said, was long.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Semicolon delimiter control: every semicolon follows a two-token item, so punctuation alone should not produce a long-unit phrase-closing peak.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Gifts received, they said, all day. The count, we heard, looked right. Nobody called.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' received' at a comma where the unit since the previous punctuation is only three tokens, so the hypothesis's length dependence predicts the floor even at a boundary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Time goes, she said, too fast. The room, we thought, felt warm. People talked.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests ' goes' at a comma with a two-token unit, again separating boundary position from unit length for a claimed trigger token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The samples remained stable throughout the entire afternoon, and the technician recorded every reading in the log.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: a novel technical sentence with an eight-token unit closing at a comma and a six-token unit before ' in'; the hypothesis predicts peaks at ' afternoon' and ' reading'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She folded the letter carefully and placed it inside the wooden drawer. The lamp, she noticed, was still burning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: narrative prose where a twelve-token unit closes at a full stop; the hypothesis predicts a peak on ' drawer' and on ' carefully' before ' and'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The first experiment failed for reasons that nobody could explain; the second produced a clear and steady signal.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: a new semicolon context with a ten-token unit before the semicolon and a five-token unit before ' and'; the hypothesis predicts peaks on ' explain' and ' clear'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The maintenance crew replaced the old valves, cracked seals and worn bearings (a job that took the whole weekend).
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: parenthetical prose where a seven-token unit closes at the closing bracket and a seven-token unit closes at the comma; the hypothesis predicts peaks on ' weekend' and ' valves'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Before the long meeting finally ended, the committee reviewed the final version of the proposal and agreed to meet again.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: procedural prose with six-token units before a comma and before ' of', plus longer units before ' and' and ' to'; the hypothesis predicts peaks on ' ended', ' version', ' proposal' and ' agreed'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The northern route proved far more difficult than anyone had expected, and we turned back at dusk without reaching the summit.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: comparative sentence with a seven-token unit before ' than' and an eleven-token unit before the comma; the hypothesis predicts peaks on ' difficult' and ' expected'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The engine started cleanly and ran smoothly for several hours but the brakes eventually failed on the hill. Nobody was hurt.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: a ten-token unit before the conjunction ' but' (and a five-token unit before ' and' after sub-word splitting); the hypothesis predicts a peak on ' hours'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The river rose steadily through the whole night and the volunteers filled more sandbags. By dawn, the water had reached the lower bridge.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: an eight-token unit before ' and' and a seven-token unit before a full stop; the hypothesis predicts peaks on ' night' and ' bridge'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Después de revisar los documentos con calma, el comité aprobó la propuesta. Al día siguiente, el director firmó el acuerdo.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: Spanish translation-style sentence whose fragments before the comma and full stop follow long units (eleven-, nine-, five- and eight-token units after sub-word splitting); the hypothesis does not restrict itself to English, so it predicts activation at those phrase-closing fragments.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Fold the mixture gently until the batter looks smooth and glossy; then pour it into the lined tin.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: recipe genre with a ten-token unit before ' and' and a thirteen-token unit before the semicolon (the closing fragment 'y' after sub-word splitting); the hypothesis predicts peaks on ' smooth' and on the semicolon-closing fragment.
